newsitem.title: UK: Britain asks rival N.Irish groups to calm down.
newsitem.headline: Britain asks rival N.Irish groups to calm down.

text.p: Britain made a plea for calm in the troubled province of Northern Ireland on Tuesday, the first anniversary of peace talks which the IRA marked by shooting at British troops.
Northern Ireland Secretary Mo Mowlam, facing a resurgent guerrilla threat and rising tension over pro-British parades, said most people wanted to live in peace.
"It is up to everybody to try and cool it. Things are very tense at the moment," she told reporters after a session of talks involving most of the province's parties in Belfast.
Mowlam said there must be no repeat of widespread conflict last year over the parades. "It is up to the people of Northern Ireland to help us to avoid that happening," she said.

The Irish Republican Army, in coded telephone calls to a local newspaper, claimed it had wounded or killed a soldier travelling past a Catholic nationalist zone in Londonderry on Tuesday. Police said however no one had been hurt.
The shooting was the guerrillas' first admitted gun attack in the city since April 10, when a sniper seriously wounded a policewoman guarding the courthouse.

It was the latest in a spate of rival guerrilla attacks casting gloom over peace talks that have struggled for life since their launch a year ago under the chairmanship of George Mitchell, a former U.S. senator.

Britain says the IRA's political wing Sinn Fein will be barred from the multi-party negotiations until the guerrillas formally end hostilities and declare a truce to replace the 17-month ceasefire they ended in February 1996.
Britain's new Labour government last month ended a 16-month ban on low-level talks with Sinn Fein after a lull in IRA violence.
But the IRA torpedoed hopes of a ceasefire on May 31 by leaving a van bomb, which did not explode, in west Belfast.
Mowlam said the Londonderry incident could have a bearing on whether her officials have a third "clarificatory meeting" soon with Sinn Fein.
"I... said all along that it will depend on the situation on the ground. But I will consider everything in-the-round and I will certainly have a look at this," Mowlam told reporters.
The IRA has killed two soldiers since last October. Their "Loyalist" foes, steadfastly opposed to the IRA's aim of ending British rule, have killed three Catholics in the past year.

Loyalist rioters, angry at a police ban on annual Protestant parades through a nearby Catholic village, injured 27 police officers and tried to burn down a Catholic church at Harryville on the outskirts of Ballymena town on Saturday night.

Catholic nationalists in Belfast demanded the abolition of anti-riot plastic bullets, blamed for the deaths of 14 civilians during years of strife, after Britain said some stocks had been withdrawn in April because their velocity was too high.
Defence Procurement Minister Lord Gilbert told parliament in London that a significant proportion of a batch of plastic bullets first issued in 1994 had been found to be defective.
